questions.question: Define the urban heat island and account for it using any three of its five causes, giving the mechanism for each.
questions.expected_answer: An urban heat island is the dome of warmer air over a city, where temperatures are noticeably higher than in surrounding rural areas, strongest at night and in winter and peaking over the city centre. Any three of: low-albedo dark surfaces absorb and store radiation by day and release it by night; anthropogenic heat from engines, industry, heating and human bodies leaks warmth into the air, peaking in winter; sealed surfaces and drained rainwater remove evaporation, so solar energy heats surfaces instead; urban canyons trap radiation between walls and let streets radiate away little heat through their narrow sky view; the pollution haze acts as a local greenhouse blanket, returning outgoing heat at night.

questions.question: Suggest four strategies to reduce the urban heat island, matching each to the cause it attacks, and state the evidence in the temperature profile that greening works.
questions.expected_answer: Light-coloured roofs and paving attack absorption by raising albedo; street trees, parks and green roofs attack the missing vegetation, cooling by shade and transpiration; permeable paving, retention ponds and wetlands attack the sealed surface by keeping water in the city for evaporation; insulation, public transport and cleaner energy attack anthropogenic heat; spacing and orienting buildings for ventilation attacks the canyon geometry. The dips in the heat-island temperature profile over parks are the evidence that vegetation cools.

questions.question: Distinguish between a pollution dome and a pollution plume, and explain how a winter temperature inversion seals the dome over a South African city.
questions.expected_answer: A pollution dome is the dome-shaped layer of polluted air that collects over a city in calm, stable conditions; when the wind rises the same pollution is drawn out downwind as a pollution plume — one pollution in two kinds of weather. On clear calm winter nights the ground cools fastest, leaving cold air beneath warmer air; rising smoke climbs only while warmer than its surroundings, so it loses buoyancy at the warm inversion layer and spreads sideways beneath it. Winter's anticyclone adds a persistent subsidence lid over the interior plateau, trapping domestic, industrial and vehicle emissions — the reason areas like the Vaal Triangle airshed are declared air-quality priority areas.
